title: Central Texas Brisket
summary: Salt, pepper, post oak, and time. The cut that sorts out who actually runs a fire.
story: In Central Texas the meat is the sauce. A packer brisket gets a Dalmatian rub, a clean oak fire, and a long ride until a probe slides in like warm butter. Bark is the whole point. Wrap only after it is set — butcher paper, not foil — so the crust survives the stall. Then rest it like you mean it. Slice the flat against the grain, turn the point, and do not apologize for the fat.

items: 1 whole packer brisket, 12–16 lb, USDA Prime or high Choice
½ cup kosher salt (Diamond Crystal; use less if Morton)
1 Tbsp granulated garlic (optional — purists skip it)
Water or melted beef tallow for spritzing
Pink butcher paper for the wrap

steps.body: Chill the brisket 30 minutes so the fat is firm. Knock off hard deckle fat, square ragged edges that will only burn, and leave about ¼ inch of fat cap. The point and flat meet at a seam — clean that up so heat can get in. Save trim for tallow.
steps.title: Trim like a butcher, not a sculptor

steps.body: Mix salt and pepper 50/50 by volume. Coat every surface, including the sides. No mustard binder needed if the meat is slightly damp. Rest uncovered in the fridge 2–12 hours if you can; overnight dry brine pays off.
steps.title: Dalmatian rub, edge to edge

steps.body: Hold 250–275°F with thin blue smoke. On an offset, feed splits before the fire starves — starving then flooding makes dirty smoke and bitter bark. Place the brisket fat-cap toward the cool side, thick end toward the firebox.
steps.title: Run a clean fire

steps.body: No peeking for the first 3–4 hours. When the color is deep mahogany and the rub no longer rubs off on a wet finger, start a light spritz every 45–60 minutes to keep the surface from drying into leather.
steps.title: Leave it alone until the bark is set

steps.body: Around 150–170°F internal the temperature stalls. Wrap in butcher paper only after the bark looks finished. Foil (the Texas crutch) speeds things up but steams the crust. Paper breathes.
steps.title: Wrap at the stall, not the clock

steps.body: Start checking at 195°F. The flat is done when a probe slides in with almost no resistance in several spots — usually 200–204°F. The point can run hotter. If it still feels tight, give it more time.
steps.title: Probe, don't worship a number

steps.body: Hold unsliced in a dry cooler or a 150°F oven at least 1 hour, 2–4 if you can. Resting finishes the cook and lets juices settle. Slice the flat against the grain, about pencil-thick. The point grain runs a different direction — turn the knife.
steps.title: Rest longer than you think

proTips.text: Dirty smoke is a fire problem, not a wood problem. If the fire is gasping, you will taste it for 14 hours. Small splits, often, with flame always visible.
Injecting is a crutch for dry flats. A Prime packer, honest trim, and a real rest beat a syringe full of phosphates.
The grain in the point turns almost 90 degrees from the flat. Find it before you slice, not after you have a board of stringy beef.

milestones.hint: Clean fire, 250–275°F, thin blue smoke.
milestones.label: On the pit

milestones.hint: Color is mahogany; rub no longer wipes off. Begin spritz.
milestones.label: Bark set

milestones.hint: Stall, 150–170°F. Wrap only if bark is finished.
milestones.label: Wrap window

milestones.hint: Like warm butter in the flat. Usually 200–204°F.
milestones.label: Probe tender

milestones.hint: 1–4 hours unsliced. This is still cooking.
milestones.label: Rest

title: Kansas City Spare Ribs
finish: Bend test; meat pulls back ~¼ inch from the bone
summary: St. Louis–cut spares, a brown-sugar rub, and a sticky molasses glaze that is Kansas City in a bone.
story: Kansas City does not pick a lane. Beef, pork, chicken, and a sauce that is tomato, molasses, and smoke. Spare ribs — trimmed to a St. Louis cut — get a sweet-savory rub, a few hours of hickory, and a glaze in the last stretch so the sugar doesn't scorch. Tender, not falling off the bone. If they collapse into mush, you steamed them.

items: 2 racks spare ribs, St. Louis cut
Yellow mustard or hot sauce, as a binder

steps.body: On the bone side, loosen the silver skin with a butter knife and pull it off with a paper towel. If you leave it, the rub never gets through and the bite is leathery.
steps.title: Peel the membrane

steps.body: Thin coat of mustard, then the rub on both sides — heavier on the meat side. Rest at room temp 30 minutes while the pit comes to 250–275°F.
steps.title: Rub and rest

steps.body: Run hickory with a little apple for sweetness. Spritz with apple juice after the first 90 minutes if the surface looks dry. Do not wrap unless you are in a hurry — unwrapped ribs keep better bark.
steps.title: Smoke bone-side down

steps.body: Classic 3-2-1 (smoke, foil, glaze) is for people who like boiled ribs. For St. Louis spares, think 4–5 hours unwrapped, then a short glaze. Foil only if they are stalling hard and dinner is waiting.
steps.title: The 3-2-1 myth

steps.body: Warm the sauce with vinegar and butter. Brush a thin coat in the last 20–30 minutes. Sugar burns; shine comes from thin layers, not a puddle.
steps.title: Glaze late

steps.body: Pick up the rack with tongs in the center. It should bend into a U and crack on the surface, not break in half. Meat retracts about ¼ inch from the bone. Rest 10 minutes, slice between bones.
steps.title: Bend, don't shred

proTips.text: Sauce is a finishing coat, not a marinade. If you need a soup of it to make the ribs taste like something, the rub and fire didn't do their job.
Judges want a clean bite mark that shows smoke ring and moisture — not bones left naked in the box.

milestones.hint: Bone-side down, 250–275°F.
milestones.label: On the pit

milestones.hint: Deep red-brown, about 2 hours. Spritz if dry.
milestones.label: Color set

milestones.hint: Thin coat, last 20–30 minutes.
milestones.label: Glaze

milestones.hint: U-shape with a surface crack. Rest 10 minutes.
milestones.label: Bend test

title: Eastern Carolina Pulled Pork
summary: A whole pork shoulder, a vinegar-pepper mop, and no tomato in sight. This is the old eastern church-picnic cook.
story: Eastern North Carolina barbecue is chopped whole hog in its purest form. For a backyard pit, a bone-in Boston butt stands in and still tells the truth: salt, pepper, vinegar, crushed red pepper, and hickory. The sauce is thin enough to drink and sharp enough to cut the fat. Serve it on a cheap bun with vinegar slaw. Do not reach for ketchup.

steps.body: Salt, pepper, paprika over the whole shoulder. No heavy brown-sugar crust — eastern sauce is the seasoning. Overnight in the fridge if you have time.
steps.title: Season simply

steps.body: Pit at 250–275°F, hickory or oak. Place fat cap up so it bastes as it renders. Expect 1½ hours per pound as a rough map, not a promise.
steps.title: Fat cap up, long smoke

steps.body: Whisk the vinegar sauce. After 4 hours, mop lightly every hour. You want a tangy bark, not a steamed roast. Keep the lid closed between mops.
steps.title: Mop after the bark sets

steps.body: Shoulders stall hard around 160°F. Wrap in paper if you need to make a window; otherwise ride it out. The collagen is still converting.
steps.title: The stall is a feature

steps.body: The blade bone should twist free with almost no effort, usually around 203°F. Rest 1 hour. Pull with your hands or cleavers, discarding the unrendered grease and the bone.
steps.title: Bone wiggle, then rest

steps.body: Chop or pull, then dress with more vinegar sauce while the meat is hot so it drinks it. Taste for salt and pepper. Serve with slaw on the side, not mixed in unless you are feeding a crowd that asked for it.
steps.title: Sauce in the pan

proTips.text: If your sauce coats a spoon, you have left the east. It should rattle in the bottle.
Mix bark and inside meat. All inside is bland; all bark is a salt bomb. The chop is the blend.

milestones.hint: Fat cap up, 250–275°F.
milestones.label: On the pit

milestones.hint: After bark sets, about 4 hours.
milestones.label: First mop

milestones.hint: Don't panic at 160°F. Wrap only if time is tight.
milestones.label: Through the stall

milestones.hint: Blade bone twists free. Rest 1 hour, then chop.
milestones.label: Bone wiggle

title: Memphis Dry Ribs
finish: Toothpick between bones with little resistance
summary: No wet sauce on the rack. A brick-red rub, hickory, and a final dusting so the spice is the crust.
story: Memphis will sell you wet ribs if you ask. The ones that made the city's name are dry: a paprika-forward rub, a hotter pit than the low-and-slow gospel, and sauce on the table if you need it. Baby backs are the usual cut. The finish is a second coat of rub so every bite starts with spice, not syrup.

items: A little oil or mustard as binder

steps.body: Peel the membrane. Oil lightly, then coat with rub. Keep a few tablespoons aside for the finish. Rest 30–60 minutes.
steps.title: Membrane off, rub on

steps.body: Memphis pits often run closer to 275–300°F. Baby backs are lean; they don't need a 6-hour funeral. Hickory only — it is the city's wood.
steps.title: Hotter than you think

steps.body: Smoke 3½–4½ hours bone-side down. Spritz with a little apple cider vinegar if the rub looks powdery-dry. Do not sauce the rack.
steps.title: No wrap, no glaze

steps.body: When a toothpick slides between bones with little push, pull them. Dust with the reserved rub while the surface is still tacky. Rest 10 minutes. Sauce on the side for the tourists.
steps.title: Dust and rest

proTips.text: The second rub is the move. Without it you just have smoked pork. With it you have a crust that smells like a spice house.
Baby backs overcook in a blink once they are close. Start probing at 3 hours and trust the toothpick, not the clock.

milestones.hint: 275°F, hickory, bone-side down.
milestones.label: On the pit

milestones.hint: Rub has melted into a crust. Spritz only if dusty.
milestones.label: Tacky bark

milestones.hint: Toothpick tender. Second rub, then rest.
milestones.label: Finish dust

title: Santa Maria Tri-Tip
summary: California's ranch-country answer to barbecue: oak coals, garlic-salt crust, salsa on the side, 90 minutes start to slice.
story: Santa Maria tri-tip is live-fire, not overnight smoke. The cut is a triangular bottom sirloin that California butchers made famous. Season with salt, garlic, and black pepper, grill over red oak, and serve with pinquito beans and a sharp salsa. It is the weeknight cook that still feels like a gathering.

items: 1 tri-tip roast, 2–3 lb, fat cap trimmed to ¼ inch
½ tsp dried parsley or rosemary (optional)

steps.body: Mix salt, garlic, pepper. Coat the roast. Look at the grain now — tri-tip grain turns in the middle. You will slice two directions later.
steps.title: Season and find the grain

steps.body: Red oak coals or a hot charcoal bed with a cool side. Sear the tri-tip 3–4 minutes per side over direct heat until a crust forms.
steps.title: Build two zones

steps.body: Move to the cool side, fat cap up, lid on. Cook to 125–130°F in the thickest part for medium-rare. Carryover will take it a few degrees more.
steps.title: Finish indirect

steps.body: Rest 15 minutes. Cut the roast in two where the grain changes, then slice each piece against the grain, ¼-inch slices. Spoon salsa over. Do not smother it.
steps.title: Rest and split the grain

proTips.text: If you treat tri-tip like brisket you will dry it out. This is a steak with a different shape. Oak and a hard sear, then get it off.
Pinquito beans belong on the plate. If you can't find them, small pink beans with a little bacon and chili powder get you close.

milestones.hint: Crust on all sides over oak coals.
milestones.label: Hard sear

milestones.hint: 125–130°F in the thickest part.
milestones.label: Indirect to temp

milestones.hint: Split at the grain change, then against the grain.
milestones.label: Slice two ways

title: Alabama White Sauce Chicken
summary: Mayonnaise, vinegar, and black pepper — the North Alabama sauce that looks wrong until you taste smoked chicken under it.
story: White sauce came out of Decatur, Alabama, as a dressing for smoked birds. It is mayonnaise thinned with cider vinegar, spiked with horseradish and a lot of black pepper. The chicken still needs real smoke and crisp skin. Sauce it off the pit so the mayo doesn't break, and serve extra in a bowl. People who swore they hated mayonnaise come back for the bottle.

items: 1 whole chicken, 4–5 lb, spatchcocked — or 4 bone-in halves

steps.body: Cut out the backbone, press the breast flat. Salt under the skin where you can. Season the skin with salt, pepper, paprika. Pit at 300–325°F — poultry likes a little more heat so the skin renders.
steps.title: Spatchcock for even heat

steps.body: Hickory or pecan, 1½–2 hours. You want rendered skin and juices that run clear. Breast 160°F, thighs 175°F. If the skin is pale, finish over direct heat 2 minutes.
steps.title: Smoke skin-side up

steps.body: It should be pourable, not a spread. Taste: more vinegar if it is flabby, more pepper if it is shy. Chill until the bird is done — cold sauce on hot chicken is the move.
steps.title: Whisk the white sauce

steps.body: Rest the chicken 10 minutes. Cut into quarters. Spoon a light coat of white sauce over, and pass the rest. Leftover sauce keeps a week and makes a smoked-turkey sandwich worth building.
steps.title: Dress and serve

proTips.text: Never cook the mayo on the bird. It breaks into grease. Smoke first, sauce second. Always.
White sauce on wings, pulled chicken, even smoked potatoes. It is not only a whole-bird dressing.

milestones.hint: 300–325°F, skin up, hickory or pecan.
milestones.label: On the pit

milestones.hint: Breast 160°F, thighs 175°F.
milestones.label: Pull temps

milestones.hint: Cold white sauce on hot chicken.
milestones.label: Dress off-pit

title: Point Burnt Ends
finish: Cubed, glazed, and sticky — about 205°F before the cube
summary: The fatty point, cubed and lacquered. Kansas City's best accident, now a destination.
story: Burnt ends used to be the dried edges pitmasters gave away. Then people got wise. Now you smoke a full packer, separate the point, cube it, and return it to the pit with sauce and sugar until the pieces are caramelized little briskets. They should bark on four sides and still be soft in the middle. If they chew like jerky, you went too far.

items: The point from a smoked packer brisket (or a 5–6 lb point, cooked like brisket first)

steps.body: Run the full brisket as in the Central Texas cook until the point is probe-tender, around 200°F. Separate the point from the flat along the seam.
steps.title: Smoke the packer first

steps.body: Cut the point into 1–1½ inch cubes. Toss with a little more rub. You want surface area — that's where the candy crust lives.
steps.title: Cube

steps.body: In a foil pan, toss cubes with sauce, brown sugar, tallow, honey. Spread in a single layer. Back on the pit at 275°F, uncovered, 45–90 minutes until the glaze is tacky and the edges have new bark.
steps.title: Pan and glaze

steps.body: Sugar goes from lacquered to ruined in a short window. Stir once. Pull when they shine and a cube compresses easily. Rest 10 minutes in the pan.
steps.title: Don't walk away

proTips.text: If you start with a lean flat you will make sad little bricks. Burnt ends are a point cook. The fat is the point.
A teaspoon of Worcestershire in the glaze pan adds the 'what is that' note without tasting like a steakhouse.

milestones.hint: Full brisket cook until the point probes like butter.
milestones.label: Point tender

milestones.hint: 1–1½ inch pieces, glaze pan, single layer.
milestones.label: Cube and sauce

milestones.hint: 45–90 minutes at 275°F until tacky, not scorched.
milestones.label: Candy bark

title: Competition Chicken Thighs
summary: The backyard version of the turn-in thigh: tight skin, mahogany color, and a glaze that doesn't slide off.
story: On the competition circuit, chicken is won or lost on skin. Rubbery skin is a zero. The trick is rendering the fat under the skin without drying the meat — a hotter pit, a little sugar in the rub, and a glaze that sets. You do not need a team trailer to cook this. You need patience with the skin and the nerve to cook thighs hotter than the internet told you.

items: 2 Tbsp melted butter or duck fat
3 Tbsp poultry rub (salt, pepper, paprika, garlic, a little brown sugar)

steps.body: Trim ragged skin and excess fat so each thigh is a tidy oval with skin covering the top — no flaps that will burn, no bald spots. Lightly score the fat under the skin with a razor if it is thick.
steps.title: Square the thighs

steps.body: Brush with melted butter. Dust with rub, including under the skin if you can without tearing it. Rest 20 minutes.
steps.title: Butter and rub

steps.body: 275–300°F, pecan or apple. About 90 minutes until the skin looks rendered and the thickest part is 165°F+. If skin is still rubbery, give it more heat, not more time at 225°F — low heat rubberizes poultry skin.
steps.title: Hotter pit, skin up

steps.body: Warm sauce with jelly and vinegar. Brush a thin coat. Another 20–30 minutes until the glaze is tacky and internal temp is 175–185°F. Rest 10 minutes. The bite should cut the skin cleanly, not pull it off in a sheet.
steps.title: Glaze to set

proTips.text: 225°F is how you make chicken skin like a rubber band. Render it. 300°F is not a crime.
Glaze should cling. If it pools on the plate, it was too thin or went on too late.

milestones.hint: Tidy ovals, skin intact, butter + rub.
milestones.label: Trim and rub

milestones.hint: 90 minutes at 275–300°F. No rubber.
milestones.label: Skin rendered

milestones.hint: Thin coat, 175–185°F, clean bite.
milestones.label: Glaze set

title: Herb-Butter Smoked Turkey
summary: A holiday bird that isn't a 12-hour hostage situation. Spatchcock, herb butter, pecan smoke, done before kickoff.
story: A whole turkey on a 225°F pit is how you serve dry breast and wait until dark. Spatchcock it, run 300°F, and butter under the skin. Pecan or apple keeps the smoke in the 'why does this taste better' range instead of ham-cured. Pull the breast at 160°F — carryover and a rest finish it. The leftovers make the sandwich that justifies the whole week.

items: 1 turkey, 12–14 lb, thawed, backbone removed and flattened
2 Tbsp kosher salt (or dry-brine the day before at ½ tsp per pound)

steps.body: Salt the turkey the day before, uncovered in the fridge. This dries the skin and seasons the meat. Spatchcock before or after brining — before is easier.
steps.title: Dry brine if you can

steps.body: Loosen the breast and thigh skin with your fingers. Push herb butter underneath in a thin layer. Rub a little on the outside with pepper and paprika.
steps.title: Butter under the skin

steps.body: Pecan or apple. Spatchcocked bird skin up. A 12–14 lb turkey often lands in 3–4 hours. Start probing the breast at 2½ hours.
steps.title: 300°F, not 225°F

steps.body: Breast 160°F, thigh 175°F. Rest 20–30 minutes tented loosely. Carryover brings the breast to a juicy 165. Slice the breast off the keel, then across the grain.
steps.title: Pull and rest

proTips.text: If the skin is brown and the breast is at 145°F, you are winning. If the skin is pale and the breast is at 165, you already lost the texture.
White sauce, burnt-end hash, or a sandwich with pickles. Do not microwave the breast — slice cold and warm in gravy.

milestones.hint: Salt overnight, uncovered, for skin that can crisp.
milestones.label: Dry brine

milestones.hint: Under the skin, then on the pit at 300°F.
milestones.label: Herb butter

milestones.hint: Breast 160°F, thigh 175°F. Rest 20 minutes.
milestones.label: Pull temps

title: Pork Belly Burnt Ends
finish: Jiggly cubes with a candy crust
summary: The shortcut burnt end: cubed pork belly, smoke, then a brown-sugar glaze. Party food that disappears first.
story: When you don't have a brisket point but you want that sticky cube, pork belly is the honest cheat. Cube it raw, season it, smoke until the fat is rendering, then glaze. Cherry wood gives them a deep color. They are rich — serve with pickles and something sharp, not more sugar on the side.

items: 4 lb skinless pork belly, cut into 1½-inch cubes
3 Tbsp pork rub (brown sugar, paprika, salt, pepper, garlic)
¼ cup honey or brown sugar

steps.body: Uniform 1½-inch cubes so they finish together. Toss with rub. Let sit 20 minutes while the pit hits 250°F.
steps.title: Cube and rub

steps.body: Set cubes on a rack over a sheet pan, not piled. Cherry or pecan, about 2½–3 hours until they look rendered and probe easily.
steps.title: Smoke on a wire rack

steps.body: Toss with warm glaze in a foil pan. Back on at 275°F, 30–45 minutes, stirring once, until lacquered. Pull before the sugar turns bitter.
steps.title: Glaze pan

steps.body: 10 minutes in the pan. Toothpicks, pickles, maybe a dust of chili flake. They seize up if they go cold — keep them warm.
steps.title: Rest and serve hot

proTips.text: Skin-on belly will never render into a burnt end. Buy skinless, or take the skin off and make chicharrones separately.
A splash of vinegar or pickle brine in the glaze pan keeps them from tasting like candy ham.

milestones.hint: 250°F on a rack, 2½–3 hours.
milestones.label: Smoke the cubes

milestones.hint: Pan, 275°F, 30–45 minutes until tacky.
milestones.label: Glaze

milestones.hint: Pickles on the side. Don't let them go cold.
milestones.label: Serve hot

title: Texas Hot Guts
summary: Coarse beef sausage, a lot of black pepper, oak smoke. The other half of a Central Texas plate.
story: Hot guts are the peppery beef links in the Hill Country — coarse grind, mustard and black pepper, stuffed in natural casings, smoked next to the brisket. Making sausage from scratch is a weekend project. Smoking good store-bought (or butcher) coarse beef links the right way is a weeknight: dry the casings, gentle oak, no rolling boil of fat. Serve with saltines and pickles, the way the halls do.

items: 2–3 lb coarse beef sausage in natural casings (or beef-pork mix)
Mustard and extra black pepper if the links are mild
Salt-and-pepper brisket drippings if you have them

steps.title: Dry the casings
steps.body: Pat the links dry and rest uncovered in the fridge 1 hour so the skin can take smoke. Wet casings stay pale.

steps.title: Don't crowd, don't prick
steps.body: 250–275°F, post oak. Lay links with space between them. Pricking dumps the fat you paid for. If one bursts, the fire was too hot or they touched.

steps.title: Pull at 160°F
steps.body: About 90–120 minutes. Casings should be bronzed and taut. Rest 10 minutes. Slice on a bias if you must; a meat-market plate is whole links.

proTips.text: If your sausage sits in a puddle, you rendered it to death. Gentle heat. The snap of the casing is the whole show.
Saltines are not a joke. They cut the grease the way bread never does.

milestones.label: Dry the casings
milestones.hint: Uncovered in the fridge so smoke will stick.

milestones.label: Gentle oak
milestones.hint: 250–275°F, space between links.

milestones.label: 160°F and snap
milestones.hint: Bronzed, taut, 10-minute rest.

title: Pit Beans with Brisket Trim
wood: Whatever is already in the fire
pitTemp: 275°F (or covered on the stovetop, then a smoke finish)
finish: Thick, glossy, smoky — beans soft, not mush
summary: Pintos, molasses, chiles, and the burnt bits you trimmed off the brisket. The side that eats like a main.
story: Pit beans should taste like they sat next to the meat, because they did. Start with dried pintos if you have the time, canned if you don't. The difference is brisket trim or burnt-end scraps, a dark molasses base, and an hour uncovered on the smoker so they pick up bark dust and smoke. They should mound on a spoon, not run.

items: 1 lb dried pinto beans, soaked overnight (or 3 cans pintos, drained)
8 oz brisket trim, burnt ends, or thick bacon, chopped
2 tsp kosher salt, plus more to finish
1 Tbsp apple cider vinegar at the end

steps.title: Brown the trim
steps.body: In a Dutch oven, render the brisket bits or bacon until they give up fat and start to crisp. Sweat onion, jalapeño, and garlic in that fat.

steps.title: Simmer
steps.body: Add beans, stock, molasses, tomato paste, mustard, and spices. Cover and cook until beans are just tender — 90 minutes for soaked dried, 20 for canned. Keep them soupy; smoke will reduce them.

steps.title: Uncovered on the pit
steps.body: Set the Dutch oven on the smoker at 275°F, no lid, 60–90 minutes. Stir the edges so they don't scorch. The top should take a little bark.

steps.title: Finish sharp
steps.body: Vinegar, more salt, maybe a pinch of brown sugar if the molasses is shy. They thicken as they sit. Serve with raw onion on top.

proTips.text: Watery beans are soup. If they won't mound, keep them on the pit. If they break into mush, you went past tender before they ever saw smoke.
Freeze brisket trim in a bag labeled 'beans.' Future you will be insufferably smug.

milestones.label: Render trim
milestones.hint: Crisp the bits, sweat the alliums.

milestones.label: Beans tender
milestones.hint: Still a little broth in the pot.

milestones.label: Uncovered smoke
milestones.hint: 60–90 minutes until they mound on a spoon.

title: Cast-Iron Smoked Mac
summary: A real cheese sauce, a cast-iron pan, and just enough smoke. Not neon-orange picnic mac.
story: Smoked macaroni and cheese is easy to ruin with too much wood and cheap cheddar that splits. Make a Mornay with extra-sharp cheddar and a little American or evaporated milk for stability, undercook the noodles, and give the pan 45 minutes next to the meat. Breadcrumbs if you want crunch. Burnt-end bits if you are showing off.

items: 1 lb elbow or cavatappi, boiled 2 minutes shy of package time
4 oz American cheese or cream cheese
½ cup panko tossed with 1 Tbsp melted butter
Optional: chopped burnt ends or jalapeño

steps.title: Make a stable sauce
steps.body: Roux the butter and flour 2 minutes. Whisk in warm milk, then evaporated milk. Off heat, melt in the cheeses. Season. It should coat a spoon.

steps.title: Undercook the pasta
steps.body: The pit is another bake. Mix noodles and sauce in a buttered 12-inch skillet. It should look a little loose.

steps.title: Smoke, don't creosote
steps.body: 275°F, a light wood. 40–50 minutes until bubbling at the edges. Add breadcrumbs for the last 15. If you want burnt ends in it, fold them in at the start.

steps.title: Rest five
steps.body: It sets as it stands. Serve from the iron. Reheats better than it has any right to.

proTips.text: Pre-shredded cheese is dusted in starch and makes a grainy sauce. Grate it. This is the whole recipe.
Mac absorbs smoke like a sponge. One chunk of apple is plenty. Hickory can turn it into an ashtray.

milestones.label: Cheese sauce
milestones.hint: Stable Mornay, noodles shy of done.

milestones.label: On the pit
milestones.hint: 275°F, light wood, 40–50 minutes.

milestones.label: Brown the top
milestones.hint: Breadcrumbs last 15 minutes. Rest 5.
